title: Why digital: noise margins, the static discipline, voltage levels for 0 and 1

items.prompt: A signal passes through twenty gates in a row and picks up a little noise on every wire. Why does the final output still come out as a clean 0 or 1?
options: Each gate outputs a fresh, full-strength 0 or 1, so noise does not build up from stage to stage.
Digital wires are shielded, so they cannot pick up noise.
The last gate has a filter that removes noise.
Noise only affects analog signals, never digital ones.
items.explanation: This is signal restoration. Every gate reads a slightly noisy input and drives its output back to a valid level, so the error does not accumulate.

options: Every gate given valid input levels must produce valid output levels, and the output levels are stricter than the input levels.
Every gate must use the same supply voltage.
No gate may change its output while the clock is high.
Every gate must have exactly two inputs.
items.explanation: Stricter output thresholds than input thresholds is what leaves room for noise: the noise margin.

items.prompt: A logic family guarantees an output low of at most V<sub>OL</sub> = 0.4 V and accepts an input low of up to V<sub>IL</sub> = 0.8 V. What is the **low noise margin** NM<sub>L</sub>?
The same family guarantees V<sub>OH</sub> = 2.4 V and requires V<sub>IH</sub> = 2.0 V. What is the **high noise margin** NM<sub>H</sub>?
A 3.3 V CMOS input is sitting at 1.6 V. How will the gate read it?
options: It is in the forbidden zone: neither a valid 0 nor a valid 1, so the output is unpredictable.
As a 0, because it is below half the supply.
As a 1, because any voltage above 1 V counts as high.
As a 0.5, because CMOS inputs are analog.
items.explanation: Between V<sub>IL</sub> and V<sub>IH</sub> the gate makes no promise. Real circuits may oscillate, draw extra current, or flip randomly.

items.prompt: Which of these are real advantages of representing information digitally rather than as a continuous analog voltage?
options: A noisy signal can be restored to a clean value at every gate.
Copies can be made with no loss at all.
Values can be stored and retrieved exactly.
A single wire carries a quantity with infinite precision.
Digital circuits always use less power than analog ones.
items.explanation: Restoration, exact copying and exact storage are the point of the digital abstraction. Precision is limited by the number of bits, and power depends on the design.

items.prompt: Put the four threshold voltages of a logic family in order from lowest to highest.
options: V<sub>OL</sub> < V<sub>IL</sub> < V<sub>IH</sub> < V<sub>OH</sub>
V<sub>IL</sub> < V<sub>OL</sub> < V<sub>OH</sub> < V<sub>IH</sub>
V<sub>OL</sub> < V<sub>OH</sub> < V<sub>IL</sub> < V<sub>IH</sub>
V<sub>IH</sub> < V<sub>IL</sub> < V<sub>OL</sub> < V<sub>OH</sub>
items.explanation: Outputs are stricter than inputs on both sides: a 0 is driven below V<sub>OL</sub> but accepted up to V<sub>IL</sub>; a 1 is driven above V<sub>OH</sub> but accepted down to V<sub>IH</sub>.

items.prompt: In 5 V TTL, V<sub>IL</sub> = 0.8 V and V<sub>IH</sub> = 2.0 V. How wide is the **forbidden zone** for inputs?
items.explanation: The forbidden zone runs from V<sub>IL</sub> to V<sub>IH</sub>: 2.0 − 0.8 = 1.2 V.

items.prompt: What does a **noise margin** actually measure?
options: How much noise a wire can pick up between one gate's output and the next gate's input while still being read correctly.
How loud the circuit is when it switches.
The difference between the supply voltage and ground.
How many gates one output can drive.
items.explanation: The margin is the gap between what a driver guarantees and what a receiver tolerates. Fan-out is a different quantity.

items.prompt: Which change to a gate design widens **both** noise margins?
options: Drive outputs closer to the supply rails: a lower V<sub>OL</sub> and a higher V<sub>OH</sub>.
Raise V<sub>IH</sub> and lower V<sub>IL</sub> so inputs are more demanding.
Lower the supply voltage without changing anything else.
Add more inputs to the gate.
items.explanation: Stronger outputs increase V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub> and V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>IH</sub> at the same time. Making inputs more demanding shrinks the margins.
